value.overview: The Hooded Warbler is a small New World warbler that breeds mainly in eastern North America and spends the nonbreeding season in Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean. It is named for the male’s striking black hood, which surrounds a bright yellow face and throat. Females are less strongly marked but retain yellow underparts and white outer tail feathers. The species is an active, mostly understory bird of forest habitats.
value.classification: The Hooded Warbler belongs to the order Passeriformes and the family Parulidae, the wood-warblers. Its scientific name is Setophaga citrina.
value.identification: Adults are about 13–15 cm long. The male has olive-green upperparts, bright yellow underparts, a yellow face, and a black hood extending around the head and throat. Females are duller, with a greenish head and a partial or weakly defined hood. In all plumages, conspicuous white outer tail spots are often flashed as the bird moves through vegetation. Its sharp chip note and ringing breeding song can also aid identification, although it is generally silent while wintering in Costa Rica.
value.rangeHabitat: The Hooded Warbler breeds across much of the eastern United States and southern Canada. It migrates through eastern and central North America and winters from eastern Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean. In Costa Rica, it occurs as a nonbreeding migrant and winter visitor rather than a resident breeding species. It is found mainly in humid lowland and foothill forests, forest edges, secondary woodland, scrub, and other habitats with dense understory, including sites in both Caribbean and Pacific regions.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds reach Costa Rica during the boreal nonbreeding season, generally from roughly September or October through March or April, with spring and fall passage birds also possible. It does not normally breed in Costa Rica.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place mainly from late spring through summer in eastern North America. The female usually builds an open cup nest low in dense shrubs or herbaceous vegetation, often in forest understory, gaps, or along edges. A typical clutch contains about three to four pale eggs marked with brown spots. The female performs most incubation and nest care, while the male defends the territory. Forest fragmentation can increase exposure to Brown-headed Cowbird brood parasitism in parts of the breeding range.
value.dietFeeding: The Hooded Warbler feeds primarily on insects and other small arthropods, including caterpillars, beetles, flies, moths, and spiders. It usually forages in shaded understory vegetation, gleaning prey from leaves and branches or making short sallies to capture insects. In winter, it may use mature forest, secondary woodland, scrub, and seasonally wet habitats. It rarely visits seed feeders because its diet is chiefly animal-based.
value.behavior: This warbler is energetic and often moves through dense vegetation close to the ground. Tail-flicking and repeated flashes of the white outer tail feathers are characteristic behaviors and may help startle hidden insects. Males and females can use somewhat different winter habitats: males tend to occupy more mature forest, while females often use scrub, secondary growth, or seasonally flooded vegetation. Hooded Warblers are territorial on their wintering grounds and usually forage alone or in loose mixed-species flocks.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered broadly stable to increasing overall, although local trends may vary among breeding and wintering regions.
